common_name: Court's Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Courtii, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and set into pure long-fiber sphagnum or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix; stand the pot permanently in a saucer of rain or distilled water and never add fertilizer or garden soil.

directions: This naturally occurring pitcher plant hybrid arises where the sprawling parrot pitcher plant (S. psittacina) grows alongside the purple pitcher plant (S. purpurea) in Gulf Coast bogs, producing decumbent, flared pitchers that blend the hooded, lobster-pot trap of one parent with the stouter, wide-mouthed form of the other. Like both parents it relies on nutrient-poor, constantly saturated acidic soil rather than fertilizer, trapping insects in its pitchers to make up the difference. Grow it in full sun in pure sphagrum or peat-sand mix kept standing in rainwater, and allow a cool winter dormancy with reduced watering so the rhizome can rest before next season's growth.

common_name: Exornata Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Exornata, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Split rhizomes in spring and pot into pure sphagnum or a peat-perlite blend, keeping the container standing in rain or distilled water year-round and avoiding any fertilized soil.

directions: A natural Gulf Coast hybrid between the pale pitcher plant (S. alata) and the purple pitcher plant (S. purpurea), this cross produces upright, trumpet-shaped pitchers in cream and maroon tones that are intermediate between its parents, variable from one wild clump to the next. As with other Sarracenia it must be grown in nutrient-starved, permanently wet acidic soil and left to catch its own insect prey rather than being fed or fertilized. Plant it in full sun for the best pitcher coloration, water only with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, and give it a true winter rest with cooler temperatures and reduced watering each year.

common_name: Formosa Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Formosa, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Separate rhizome divisions in spring into pure long-fiber sphagnum or a peat-perlite mix kept standing in rainwater; this low-growing hybrid resents mineral-rich tap water and fertilizer alike.

directions: Where the hooded pitcher plant (S. minor) overlaps with the parrot pitcher plant (S. psittacina) in Southeastern bogs, this low, clumping natural hybrid results, bearing short, decumbent pitchers with a partly hooded, partly flared opening that reflects both parents. It survives on the same nutrient-poor, waterlogged acidic soil its parents need, capturing insects in its pitchers since the surrounding bog substrate has almost nothing for roots to absorb. Keep it in full sun, stand the pot in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times, and let it go dormant with cold, drier conditions over winter for healthy long-term growth.

common_name: Gilpin's Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Gilpinii, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring and replant into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-and-perlite mix sitting in a saucer of rain water; never allow the medium to dry out or receive fertilizer.

directions: This natural hybrid forms where the sprawling parrot pitcher plant (S. psittacina) meets the sweet pitcher plant (S. rubra) in coastal plain bogs, giving rise to plants with slender, upright-to-decumbent pitchers and a partially closed hood that is more pronounced than in either parent alone. Its roots live in the same nutrient-starved, saturated peat that both parents require, so it depends on trapping insects in its pitchers rather than drawing nutrition from the soil. Grow it in full sun with its roots permanently wet in rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, and give it a cold, low-water dormancy each winter to mimic its native bog conditions.

common_name: Harper's Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Harperi, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring into pure long-fiber sphagnum or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix kept standing in rain water; avoid garden soil and any fertilizer, which will kill the fine roots.

directions: A natural cross between the yellow trumpet pitcher plant (S. flava) and the hooded pitcher plant (S. minor), this hybrid occurs in Southeastern seepage bogs and produces tall, narrow-hooded pitchers in pale yellow-green with a tightly arched lid that shades the trap opening more than S. flava's does alone. Like its parents it is adapted to acidic, mineral-poor, permanently wet soil and feeds itself by trapping insects that are drawn into the pitcher and cannot climb back out past the waxy inner walls. Site it in full sun for the strongest pitcher color, water only with rain or distilled water, and allow a cold winter dormancy with reduced moisture to keep the rhizome healthy year after year.

common_name: Rehder's Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Rehderi, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Split rhizome divisions in spring into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix standing in a tray of rain water, keeping the medium acidic and free of fertilizer or mineral-rich tap water.

directions: Found where the hooded pitcher plant (S. minor) and the sweet pitcher plant (S. rubra) grow side by side in Southeastern bogs, this natural hybrid bears slender, upright pitchers with a narrowly arched hood that is intermediate between its parents' forms, often flushed with maroon veining. It lives in the same waterlogged, nutrient-poor peat its parents require and must trap insects to supplement what the soil cannot provide. Grow it in full sun with roots standing permanently in rain or distilled water, and give it a true cold-season rest with less water each winter so it can resume vigorous pitcher production the following spring.

planting.note: Root leaf pullings in a mineral mix of sand, perlite, and peat watered only with distilled or rain water; this hybrid tolerates slightly drier footing than true bog carnivores but still needs nutrient-poor, acidic soil.

directions: Bred from Pinguicula agnata and selected for an unusually large summer rosette, Titan is among the biggest of the Mexican butterwort hybrids, its broad, sticky-surfaced leaves trapping gnats and fungus flies over a wide carnivorous rosette before stalks of pale lavender flowers rise above the foliage. Give it bright filtered light, a well-drained mineral mix of sand, perlite, and peat kept evenly moist with distilled or rain water, and never fertilize the soil, since mineral buildup damages the roots. Allow a winter rest with reduced water as the plant shrinks into a smaller, non-carnivorous succulent rosette, resuming full growth once longer days return.

common_name: Weser Butterwort (Pinguicula moranensis x ehlersiae Hybrid)

planting.note: Propagate from leaf pullings set into a peat-sand-perlite mix and water with distilled or rain water; keep the mix evenly moist in the growing season and nearly dry during winter dormancy.

directions: One of the older German-raised Mexican butterwort hybrids, Weser was created by crossing Pinguicula moranensis with P. ehlersiae and is grown for its unusually large, deep purplish flowers held well above a rosette of flypaper-like, insect-trapping leaves. It needs the same acidic, mineral-poor substrate as its wild parents, so pot it in a peat-sand-perlite blend and water only with distilled or rain water, never tap water or fertilizer. In cooler months it pulls back into a tight, non-sticky succulent winter rosette and should be watered sparingly until vigorous summer growth resumes.

planting.note: Root leaf pullings in a sand-perlite-peat mix kept moist with distilled or rain water; this hybrid multiplies readily from pullings and offsets, making it one of the easier Mexican butterworts to propagate.

directions: A complex Mexican butterwort hybrid in the Pinguicula agnata-moranensis-ehlersiae group, Pirouette is prized among growers for being especially fast and easy to multiply, forming offset rosettes of sticky, insect-trapping leaves topped by stalks of pale pink to lavender flowers. It wants the same bright, humid, and acidic growing conditions as its Mexican highland parents: a mineral sand-perlite-peat mix watered only with distilled or rain water and never fertilized. Expect it to shrink into a smaller succulent rosette through a cooler, drier winter rest before flushing back into vigorous carnivorous growth in spring.

common_name: Tina Butterwort (Pinguicula agnata x zecheri Hybrid)

planting.note: Set rooted leaf pullings into a mineral peat-sand-perlite blend and irrigate only with distilled or rain water, letting the mix stay evenly moist through the growing season.

directions: Originated from a cross between Pinguicula agnata and P. zecheri, Tina is a compact Mexican butterwort grown for its neat rosette of sticky, insect-catching leaves and its pale flowers carried on slender stalks above the foliage. Because it comes from highland Mexican parents, it needs very bright filtered light, a nutrient-poor mineral mix of peat, sand, and perlite, and watering with distilled or rain water rather than tap water or fertilizer. Reduce watering in winter so the plant can pull into a smaller, non-carnivorous resting rosette, then resume normal watering as new sticky summer leaves emerge.

common_name: John Rizzi Butterwort (Large-Flowered Mexican Pinguicula Hybrid)

planting.note: Root leaf pullings in a sand-perlite-peat mix and water only with distilled or rain water; keep humidity high and avoid any fertilizer or mineral-rich water that can burn the fine roots.

directions: Named for the American grower who first distributed it, John Rizzi is a Mexican butterwort hybrid valued for its oversized leaves and showy flowers, which open noticeably larger than those of many related moranensis-group hybrids. Its sticky summer rosette traps small flying insects while its roots sit in the same nutrient-poor, acidic mineral mix its wild Mexican relatives require, so pot it in sand, perlite, and peat watered only with distilled or rain water. Give it bright, humid, filtered-light conditions through the growing season and a cooler, drier winter rest, during which the rosette contracts before flushing back out the following spring.

planting.note: Scatter small divisions or plugs onto the surface of a constantly saturated peat-sand mix or milled sphagnum; never fertilize or use mineral-rich water on this nutrient-poor substrate.

directions: Selected from a wild population at Betty's Bay in South Africa's Western Cape, this terrestrial bladderwort form is grown for flowers far larger and showier than the typical weedy bisquamata, with a bright yellow palate set against a broad lilac lower lip, blooming almost continuously through the warm season. Like all terrestrial Utricularia it has no true roots and instead catches microscopic soil organisms with tiny underground bladder traps, drawing essentially nothing from the substrate itself. Grow it in shallow trays of constantly wet, nutrient-poor peat-sand mix or sphagnum under bright, humid, partially shaded conditions, watering only with rain or distilled water, and it will spread by fine runners to carpet the pot.

planting.note: Divide crowns or root leaf-tip cuttings into a wet peat-sand mix kept standing in rain or distilled water; this hybrid is maintained only by vegetative propagation, not by seed.

directions: Bred in 1973 by carnivorous plant hobbyist Joseph Mazrimas by crossing the temperate threadleaf sundew (D. filiformis) with its Gulf Coast relative (D. tracyi), this long-established hybrid produces tall, upright, thread-like leaves densely covered in glistening, dew-tipped tentacles that flush rosy red in strong sun, giving the hybrid its name. Like both parents it grows in nutrient-poor, constantly wet acidic bog soil and depends on trapping small flying insects on its sticky leaves rather than on fertile soil. Plant it in full sun in a peat-sand mix kept standing in rainwater, and allow a cooler winter dormancy with reduced watering, since it is propagated only by division or cuttings and does not come true from seed.
